item.title: Distributed Nested Coevolutionary Architecture and Approach for Multiobjective Scheduling of Agile Earth Observation Satellite
item.description: As the escalating demands for Earth observation and the increasing diversification of user requirements, agile Earth observation satellites (AEOSs) have been widespread deployed to leverage their superior attitude maneuverability. This leads to a multiobjective AEOS scheduling problem (MO-AEOSSP). The complex time-dependent transition of satellite attitudes between consecutive observations further increases the challenge of the problem. To address the MO-AEOSSP, this article proposes a new approach called the nested distributed coevolutionary algorithm (NDCEA). In particular, an objective-driven heuristic initialization strategy is designed to generate a superior exploration population, and the nondominated individuals are selected to generate an independent population for exploitation. During the evolutionary process, the exploration is executed by a newly devised discrete differential evolution (DDE) algorithm, in which algebraic operators are problem-specifically redefined, and a repair operator is developed to transform the generated infeasible individuals into feasible ones. Exploitation is implemented in a distributed way with the exploration campaign. To fully utilize the superior information of nondominated individuals, the exploitation population is adaptively divided into a convergent population and a diverse population at each generation. They are also coevolved in a distributed way by multiple objective-driven local enhancement strategies. Hence, a nested distributed coevolutionary architecture is constructed and employed in NDCEA. After the exploration and exploitation are completed, a decomposition-based selection strategy is designed to construct superior next-generation populations. Finally, NDCEA is comprehensively assessed against the exact mathematical model on five small-scale instances and compared with state-of-the-art multiobjective algorithms on eight large-scale instances. The experimental results demonstrate the significant superiority of NDCEA over the compared approaches, thereby confirming its efficacy for the considered problem.
item.authors: Guanghui Zhang;Chenxuan Wei;Haoyu Zhao;Lijie Zhang;Guangyun Zhang;

item.title: A Cloud’s Droplet Size—and Its Internal Structure—From Monochrome Multiangle Imaging
item.description: Cloud droplet size plays a key role in precipitation formation, the cloud radiative effect, and the coupling of clouds to atmospheric turbulence. Due to this confluence of processes, measurements of droplet size are critical to our understanding of the climate system. Satellite remote sensing is the primary means of collecting these measurements over the globe and it is generally considered that multispectral or polarized measurements are required to isolate droplet size from droplet concentration. Here, we challenge this paradigm. We hypothesize that key information about the droplet size is encoded in the multiscale structure of multiangle imagery enabling the retrieval of droplet size from monochrome nonpolarized measurements in the visible (VIS) spectrum. We prove this hypothesis using forward and inverse (i.e., tomographic) 3-D radiative transfer (RT) modeling based on realistic cloud models. We demonstrate that a vertical profile of droplet effective radius and the 3-D volume extinction coefficient of the cloud can be retrieved using high-resolution ( $\lesssim \!\!50$ m) imagery at nine viewing angles using only the red channel. We attribute this success to the turbulent nature of cumuliform clouds that produces tenuous, optically thin regions at cloud edge that are only detectable at high spatial resolution. Observations of these regions are sensitive to scattering phase function (PF), hence to droplet size, due to the dominance of low-order scattering. Finally, we verify that the addition of multispectral measurements in the shortwave infrared improves the tomographic retrieval of both the 1-D droplet effective radius profile and the 3-D extinction coefficient field through their improved sensitivity to regions where higher-order scattering dominates.
item.authors: Anthony B. Davis;Kailen A. Hargenrader;Linda Forster;Jesse R. Loveridge;Marcin J. Kurowski;Aviad Levis;

item.title: UAV-Borne Quasi-3-D Observation of Physical–Biological Coupling in a Dipole Eddy by Integrating Radar Altimetry and Ocean LiDAR
item.description: 3-D remote sensing of the upper ocean remains a major challenge in ocean observation. Conventional dynamic remote sensing can effectively detect sea surface height (SSH), but it lacks the capability to synchronously sense subsurface structures, which limits observations of 3-D physical and biogeochemical variability in the upper ocean. To address this limitation, we develop an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-borne quasi-3-D remote sensing system that integrates a dual-frequency Ka/Ku radar altimeter and a dual-wavelength blue–green ocean light detection and ranging (LiDAR) system. A flight campaign of over 5800 km was carried out over a mesoscale dipole eddy in the northern South China Sea (SCS), enabling synchronous high-resolution measurements of sea level anomaly (SLA) and subsurface chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) profiles. The SLA retrieved from UAV-borne radar altimetry agreed with the 0.25° Data Unification and Altimeter Combination System (DUACS) and Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) 2-km products, with root-mean-square errors of 0.44 and 0.51 cm and mean biases of +0.006 and −0.001 cm, respectively. The Chl-a profiles retrieved from UAV-borne LiDAR agreed with synchronous in situ fluorescence observations, with an RMSE of $0.071~\mu $ g $\cdot $ L−1, an MAE of $0.067~\mu $ g $\cdot $ L−1, and a mean bias of $+ 0.067~\mu $ g $\cdot $ L−1. These synchronous observations further revealed the coupled physical and bio-optical structure of the dipole eddy, showing that an approximately 10 cm decrease in SLA coincided with an approximately 12 m shoaling of the subsurface chlorophyll maximum (SCM) and an approximately $0.15~\mu $ g $\cdot $ L−1 increase in subsurface Chl-a. These results support the feasibility of synchronous quasi-3-D sensing of upper ocean dynamical and bio-optical structure and inform the development of future spaceborne 3-D ocean remote sensing missions.
item.authors: Fangjie Yu;Ziliang Jiang;Junwu Tang;Hanwei Sun;Hongwei Zhang;Yan He;Ziming Gao;Zetao Hu;Mengke Ren;Xinglong Zhang;Songhua Wu;Ge Chen;

item.title: Quantifying Urban–Rural Drought in Africa Using a PCA-Based Multisensor Drought Stress Ratio
item.description: Building climate-resilient adaptation in rapidly urbanizing African regions requires a deeper understanding of drought dynamics across interconnected urban and rural systems. This study develops a remote sensing-based framework to quantify the relative dominance of urban water–energy demand stress and rural agricultural drought across Africa. The urban–rural drought stress ratio (URDSR) is proposed, which is a novel principal component analysis (PCA)-based multisensor drought diagnostic that separates urban anthropogenic water–energy demand stress from rural hydroclimatic agricultural drought within a unified framework. Multisensor observations from Sentinel-1/2, Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS), and Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) are harmonized to monthly 0.05° grids. PCA is applied to construct two sectoral indices: an urban water demand index (Uw) representing infrastructure- and temperature-driven urban water pressure, and the rural stress index (Rs) representing agricultural drought derived from vegetation and hydrological deficits. Their contrast forms URDSR, enabling dynamic assessment of the balance between urban and rural drought stress. The framework is evaluated against conventional drought indicators, including the standardized precipitation index (SPI) and standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) derived from CHIRPS data, with detailed analysis for Cairo, Lagos, Nairobi, Khartoum, Addis Ababa, and Johannesburg. Validation against benchmark indices [SPI, SPEI, vegetation health index (VHI), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), vegetation condition index (VCI), and temperature–vegetation dryness index (TVDI)] shows strong correlations (r = 0.70–0.85, p < 0.01), revealing a south–north transition from rural-dominated to increasingly urban drought regimes.
item.authors: Nasser A. M. Abdelrahim;Shuanggen Jin;Shiyu Li;

item.title: STSTFN: Spatiotemporal–Spectral Land Surface Temperature Fusion Network
item.description: Land Surface Temperature (LST) plays a crucial role in climate change research, ecological monitoring, and agricultural management. However, acquiring LST data with both fine temporal and fine spatial resolution remains a significant challenge. Existing downscaling methods are primarily constrained by insufficient capture of fine spatial details, and error accumulation inherent in multistep processing. To overcome these limitations and achieve robust, end-to-end LST downscaling, this article proposes a deep learning-based Spatiotemporal–spectral fusion network (STSTFN), which uses MODIS and Landsat LST products as base data and incorporates Sentinel-2’s near infrared (NIR) band as auxiliary input to enhance spatial detail. A multiscale convolutional fusion network is employed to learn the nonlinear mappings between the input and output data, enabling finer reconstruction of LST. Furthermore, STSTFN introduces a bi-temporal fusion strategy using a blur-weight difference-based weighting mechanism, which effectively integrates predictions from both temporal directions. Compared with a traditional method [spatiotemporal integrated temperature fusion model (STITFM)], and two deep learning-based methods [two-stage hierarchical spatiotemporal fusion network (THSTNet), and spatiotemporal temperature fusion network (STTFN)], STSTFN demonstrated superior performance in both quantitative evaluation (achieving an average root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.68°, a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.936, and a correlation coefficient (CC) of 0.931, which represent improvements of 32.9%, 6.2%, and 3.6% over the compared methods, respectively) and visual assessments, confirming its effectiveness and superiority in generating high-quality LST products.
item.authors: Hao Wu;Guochen Xie;Zhixiang Yin;Jingan Wu;Penghai Wu;

item.title: STICCD: Spatiotemporal Feature Integration and Cascaded Change Decoding for Superresolution Mapping
item.description: Spatiotemporal superresolution mapping (STSRM) aims to generate fine-resolution (FR) land cover maps from coarse-resolution (CR) observations by leveraging prior FR land cover maps. However, most existing STSRM methods still cannot effectively exploit the spatial details contained in prior FR information, which limits the recovery of fine structures in the predicted FR results. Here, we propose spatiotemporal feature integration and cascaded change decoding (STICCD), a STICCD framework, to couple bitemporal CR fraction variations with prior FR spatial details for target-time FR land cover reconstruction. In STICCD, an adaptive cross-source spatiotemporal feature integration module (STIM) is designed to jointly model the interactions between bitemporal CR fraction variations and prior FR spatial details, thereby constructing a unified representation for subsequent decoding. On this basis, a change localization (CL) and transition decoding strategy is introduced to progressively recover land cover transitions. The binary localization branch first identifies candidate changed regions to reduce the interference of the dominant unchanged background, and the transition decoding branch further determines class-to-class transitions within these regions. The final target-time FR land cover map is then reconstructed by updating the prior FR land cover map according to the predicted changes. Experiments on simulated datasets derived from the US National Land Cover Database (NLCD) and on real mangrove mapping using Sentinel-2 and Planet imagery demonstrate that STICCD consistently outperforms competing methods in both quantitative accuracy and spatial reconstruction quality, particularly in preserving fine-scale structures, complex boundaries, and land cover transitions.
item.authors: Xingling Wu;Zhixiang Yin;Jie Lu;Xinyan Li;Penghai Wu;Feng Ling;

item.title: FastSAM-Guided Adversarial Learning for Unsupervised Multimodal Remote Sensing Change Detection
item.description: Multimodal change detection (CD), due to its ability to flexibly adapt to data acquired from different types of sensors, has become an important research direction in the field of remote sensing. However, existing methods generally lack feature representations with sufficient generalization capacity, leading to pronounced performance degradation when applied across diverse scenes. To address this limitation, we propose a novel FastSAM-guided adversarial learning (FastSAM-GAL) framework for unsupervised multimodal CD. The proposed framework effectively mitigates cross-modal discrepancies via adversarial learning and constructs a dual-branch architecture comprising a FastSAM encoder and a remote sensing encoder, thereby fully exploiting the complementary information between generic visual semantic features and domain-specific remote sensing representations to substantially enhance cross-scene generalization capability. Furthermore, a progressive multiscale perception adaptor (PMSPA) and a spatial-frequency collaborative edge augmentation (SFCEA) module are specifically designed to further improve FastSAM-GAL’s ability to perceive objects at different scales and capture change boundaries. Finally, comparative experiments on five real-world multimodal CD datasets against 12 state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that the proposed FastSAM-GAL maintains stable and reliable detection performance across multimodal remote sensing data with diverse scenes, with its $\kappa $ metric significantly outperforming all competing methods.
item.authors: Zhifu Zhu;Xiping Yuan;Shu Gan;Weidong Luo;Cheng Chen;Xuan Li;

item.title: MV-MoE: A Multiview Expert Fusion Framework for Multispectral Object Detection
item.description: Multimodal image fusion, particularly the collaborative modeling of infrared and visible light images, plays a crucial role in tasks such as nighttime target perception and visual enhancement. Although existing methods have enhanced the expressive capabilities of multimodal information fusion to some extent, they struggle to fully construct the multiperspective semantic structures inherent in different modalities. This results in a lack of controllability in fusion pathways, insufficient information coordination, and a high susceptibility to semantic conflicts. To address this, we propose a fusion framework of a mixture of experts based on multiview parallel expert groups (MV-MoE). This framework enables path modeling and expert activation scheduling within a hierarchical structure. The method establishes multiperspective semantic expert groups driven by a hierarchical dynamic gating mechanism, enabling perspective selection and adaptive data fusion during feature extraction. The core approach involves concatenating multisource data features and feeding them into a hierarchical parallel expert network to extract multiview feature information. A dynamic gating mechanism then weights and fuses feature results from different perspectives, enabling multiview feature extraction and dynamic fusion of multimodal data. Building upon this foundation, an intragroup collaborative regularization strategy is introduced to enhance coordination and generalization capabilities among expert networks, ensuring stability and reliability in fusion. Concurrently, a globally shared expert module is incorporated to balance multiview detail information with holistic context, further improving consistency in the fusion process and stability in object detection. Extensive experimental validation across multiple datasets conclusively demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The code is available at https://github.com/AnWiLL-Work/MV-Moe.git
item.authors: Yongan Lu;Renbo Luo;Yihan Yao;Jialing Lian;Guohao Liao;Zhifeng Wu;

item.title: Make Some Noise: Unsupervised Remote Sensing Change Detection Using Latent-Space Perturbations
item.description: Unsupervised change detection (UCD) aims to localize changes between two images of the same region without relying on labeled training data. Most recent approaches either use a frozen foundation model in a training-free manner or train with synthetic changes generated in pixel space. Both strategies inherently rely on predefined assumptions about change types, typically introduced through handcrafted rules, external datasets, or auxiliary generative models. Due to these assumptions, such methods fail to generalize beyond a few change types, limiting their real-world usage, especially in rare or complex scenarios. To address this, we propose make some noise (MaSoN), an end-to-end UCD framework that synthesizes diverse changes directly in the latent feature space during training. It generates changes dynamically estimated from feature statistics of the target data, enabling diverse yet data-driven variation aligned with the target domain. Since synthesis happens in latent space, it also easily extends to new modalities, such as SAR and multispectral data. MaSoN generalizes strongly across diverse change types and improves the average $F1$ -score across five benchmarks by 14.1 percentage points (p.p.). Project page: https://blaz-r.github.io/mason_ucd/
item.authors: Blaž Rolih;Matic Fučka;Filip Wolf;Luka Čehovin Zajc;

item.title: A Multifrequency SAR Tomography Method via Mixed-Norm and Deep Unfolding Network
item.description: Tomographic synthetic aperture radar (TomoSAR) enables 3-D imaging of observed scenes while typically requiring numerous flight passes to achieve high-quality imaging and avoid elevation ambiguities. Recently developed multifrequency TomoSAR (MF-TomoSAR) offers a promising approach to reduce the required flight passes by expanding the effective spatial-frequency sampling in the elevation direction. However, existing MF-TomoSAR approaches fail to preserve frequency-dependent scattering information and are computationally demanding, as they lack explicit per-frequency scattering modeling and require tedious hyperparameter tuning. To address these limitations, this article proposes a mixed-norm multifrequency (MMFreq) TomoSAR imaging framework, and the main contributions are threefold. First, the MMFreq imaging model is proposed, which incorporates a mixed-norm regularization to jointly characterize cross-frequency scattering features while preserving per-frequency scattering information. Second, MMFreq-three-operator splitting (TOS) is derived as an efficient imaging algorithm based on the TOS framework, which provides closed-form update rules for the MMFreq model. Third, MMFreq-Net is developed as a deep unfolding network (DUN) that maps the MMFreq-TOS algorithm into a learnable architecture, achieving faster imaging and automatic parameter optimization. Finally, real-data experiments successfully yield unambiguous 3-D imaging results at each frequency, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed MMFreq framework.
item.authors: Peiyao Liu;Zegang Ding;Zhen Wang;Yuewen Yang;Jian Zhao;Ziyi Zhou;Zhicheng Xie;Yiyi Ren;

item.title: A Multicondition Normalized BRDF Correction Framework for Inland Water Bodies Using Airborne Hyperspectral Imagery
item.description: The bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) effects in airborne hyperspectral images can generate severe brightness gradients and radiometric inconsistency over inland water bodies, hindering precise quantitative applications. This challenge is particularly acute for lightweight airborne hyperspectral systems, where multistrip acquisition and frequent attitude fluctuations can amplify water-surface specular reflection and scattering, resulting in severe radiometric inconsistencies. We propose a unified BRDF correction framework for inland water bodies, driven by the normalization of multiple imaging conditions. By physically decoupling high-frequency sensor attitude fluctuations from periodic sensor heading systemic shifts, and constructing a kernel-based semiempirical model optimized for the complex anisotropic scattering mechanisms of inland water, this framework reduces radiometric distortions induced by dynamic attitude variations and characterizes water-body BRDF properties. By conducting an overall homogeneity visual interpretation of the mosaicked images and quantitatively calculating the reflectance of overlapping regions, we demonstrate that the correction reduces BRDF-induced radiometric inconsistency. Specifically, the mean absolute difference (MAD) of water reflectance in overlapping areas is reduced by over 50%. Evaluated against ground-measured spectra, the coefficient of determination (R ${}^{2}$ ) of the corrected reflectance reaches over 0.9. Compared with traditional BRDF correction methods, the proposed framework achieves superior performance in both visual effect and quantitative evaluation. Through comparative validation from different regions, the robustness and accuracy of the model are further demonstrated, providing precise data support for subsequent high-precision quantitative inversion and mapping. With the trend of lightweight airborne imaging systems, the proposed BRDF correction framework offers a robust radiometric baseline and has extensive application prospects for hyperspectral applications.
item.authors: Chao Niu;Kun Tan;Xue Wang;Yan Huang;Peijun Du;

item.title: Image-Domain Deep-Learning LSRTM With Multiscale Degradation Modulation and Forward Reconstruction Consistency
item.description: Reverse time migration (RTM) images are jointly constrained by limited acquisition aperture, band-limited source wavelets, and errors in the background velocity model. These factors often cause spatially varying resolution loss, uneven illumination, and amplitude distortion. These problems are more obvious in deep structures and poorly illuminated areas. Data-domain least-squares RTM (LSRTM) improves imaging resolution effectively. However, repeated migration and demigration lead to high computational cost and low efficiency. To address this problem, this article proposes an image-domain learning-based LSRTM (DL-ID-LSRTM) framework. The framework introduces degradation information related to migration conditions as conditional constraints during inversion. A forward reconstruction consistency (FRC) constraint is also introduced to improve image-domain consistency. In particular, the proposed method fuses the migration velocity model with a point spread function (PSF) descriptor. These inputs parameterize local degradation features caused by migration. These features depict local focusing behavior and illumination patterns. A spatially adaptive feature modulation (SAFM) mechanism then injects these conditional features into a multiscale inversion backbone. This design guides reflectivity reconstruction. In addition, this article designs a closed-loop forward reconstruction branch. Under the same migration conditions, the predicted reflectivity is used to synthesize an RTM profile, and an image-domain consistency loss is imposed between this synthesized profile and the input RTM image. This design suppresses shortcut learning and reduces nonphysical artifacts. Results from benchmark tests on two synthetic datasets, one out-of-distribution generalization experiment, and one marine field dataset support the proposed method. Compared with RTM, U-Net-based image-domain LSRTM, and data-domain LSRTM with a limited number of iterations, DL-ID-LSRTM produces estimates closer to subsurface reflectivity features. The results show improved lateral reflector continuity, restored amplitudes in weakly illuminated deep zones, reduced migration-related smearing, and a more balanced relative amplitude distribution with depth.

item.title: 3-D Inversion of Airborne Electromagnetic Data Based on Adaptive Octree Meshes
item.description: Airborne electromagnetic (AEM) inversion is a key approach for reconstructing subsurface resistivity structures in geologically complex regions. Owing to the complexity of subsurface media, the conventional 1-D and 2-D inversion approaches are insufficient for resolving these geological structures. The development of fully 3-D inversion methodologies is necessary. However, in large-scale 3-D AEM inversions, the structured meshes impose severe limitations on local refinement, constraining mesh design and parameterization. Here, we present a 3-D inversion framework for AEM data based on an adaptive octree discretization. The forward and adjoint modeling are performed using a vector finite-element (FE) formulation on octree meshes, enabling flexible local meshes guided by the system footprint and thereby reducing degrees of freedom while improving computational efficiency. An adaptive mesh-refinement strategy is further incorporated to dynamically balance inversion accuracy and computational cost. Synthetic experiments demonstrate that the adaptive octree approach outperforms the conventional uniform-mesh strategies in recovering anomaly geometry, delineating structural boundaries and reducing computational expenses. Application to an AEM field dataset acquired from the Lofoten–Vesterlen region of Norway successfully resolves multiple conductive structures that are consistent with prior geological knowledge, confirming the robustness and suitability of the method for large-scale surveys. These results highlight the potential of octree-based adaptive inversion to substantially enhance both accuracy and efficiency in 3-D AEM imaging.
item.authors: Jianfu Ni;Xue Han;Changchun Yin;Xinru Guo;Bo Zhang;Luyuan Wang;Vikas Chand Baranwal;

item.title: 3-D Joint Inversion of Gravity and Magnetotelluric Data Based on Gaussian Mixture Model Clustering Constraints
item.description: Joint inversion is an effective approach for reducing the nonuniqueness of geophysical inversion by integrating complementary information from different datasets. This study builds upon the petrophysically and geologically guided inversion (PGI) framework and applies a fixed-prior Gaussian mixture model (GMM) formulation to 3-D joint inversion of gravity and magnetotelluric (MT) data. In this framework, quantitative information on petrophysical classes and global prior probabilities is represented by a GMM in the joint physical-property space, and the GMM-based petrophysical regularization replaces the traditional least-squares model regularization term of the objective function. The GMM parameters in this study are estimated before the inversion and kept fixed during the inversion. To construct the prior GMM, the component means and proportions are obtained from labeled prior samples, and the within-component variability is represented by user-specified Gaussian perturbations. The resulting covariance matrices are then estimated using Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage estimation. This provides a practical way to construct the fixed-prior GMM and reduces the need for repeated trial-and-error inversions. Four synthetic examples are used to evaluate the joint inversion workflow of gravity and MT data. The results show that the fixed-prior GMM constraint can guide the joint inversion toward models consistent with the prescribed petrophysical classes and global prior probabilities. Compared with single-method inversions, the fixed-prior GMM-constrained workflow improves the consistency between recovered residual density and resistivity structures and enhances the recovery of target bodies.
